Enemy State Machines

Every enemy you build this year — the patrolling guard, the turret that shoots, the boss with three phases — is the same idea: a thing with a small set of behaviors, one of which is active, and the conditions that trade between them. This is the pattern reference, from the guard in Unit 4 to the boss in Unit 8.

What a state machine IS (in AP words)

A state machine is state stored in fields (1.3a), selection choosing between behaviors (AAP-3), and Update providing the iteration that asks the conditions over and over. The exam's definition of an algorithm — sequencing, selection, iteration — lives inside every enemy controller in the starter, and you can point at each one: 

private void Update()                         // ITERATION (60×/sec)
{
    if (isPlatformer)                         // SELECTION
    {
        PlatformerMove();                     // SEQUENCING: which behavior
    }
    else
    {
        TopDownMove();
    }
}

The guard's machine (Unit 4)

The starter's EnemyController implements a machine whose states are mostly implicit — they exist as conditions, not as a named enum:

StateWhere it lives in the codeTransitions
PATROLthe else of the chase condition / PlatformerMove→ CHASE when distance < chaseDistance
CHASEthe if in TopDownMove→ PATROL when the player is out of range
ATTACKOnCollisionEnter2D / Stay2D → TryDamagefires during either move state, on a cooldown

The elegant part: there is no "return to patrol" line anywhere. The chase sits inside an if; when the if stops matching, the enemy simply falls back to its default behavior. The patrol was never switched OFF — it was outvoted. Drawn on paper (4.5a), the machine is four boxes and three arrows; coded, it is three ifs and a cooldown.

The turret, minimized

Even the turret is a two-state machine: SHOOTING (in range AND off cooldown) and WAITING — and the cooldown pattern (3.3a) is what turns "in range" into a rhythm. A timer plus a comparison IS a state machine with a clock for a brain. This is why the cooldown pattern reappears everywhere: attack rates, contact damage, jump mercies (6.3a), turn gates (10.2d).

Making states explicit (the enum upgrade)

When a machine grows past "a couple of ifs," named states earn their ceremony. The starter style would keep it simple: 

private enum BossState { Idle, Attacking, Recovering, Dead }
private BossState state = BossState.Idle;

private void Update()
{
    switch (state)                              // explicit selection
    {
        case BossState.Idle:
            state = BossState.Attacking;        // a transition
            break;
        case BossState.Attacking:
            FireShockwave();
            state = BossState.Recovering;
            break;
        case BossState.Recovering:
            if (Time.time >= lastAttackTime + attackInterval)
            {
                state = BossState.Idle;
            }
            break;
    }
}

Two rules make explicit machines trustworthy: one state active at a time (if two can be active, you did not need a state machine), and every transition has a condition you can read aloud ("recovering ends when the interval has elapsed"). A machine whose transitions you cannot narrate is a pile of ifs wearing a costume.

The boss's phase layer (Unit 8)

The boss stacks a second machine ON TOP of the behavior one: phases — a one-way ladder driven by health thresholds (8.2a). Two design facts make phases work:

  • Phase changes fire DOWNWARD ONLY (currentPhase guards in the threshold check), so a phase entrance never re-runs
  • Phase changes swap NUMBERS via a phase table (8.4a) — cooldowns, speeds, attack sets — so the player SEES difficulty change without a single new mechanic being taught

A phase is "the same machine with different constants" — which is also the exam's cleanest example of managing complexity: one table, one switch statement, six difficulty knobs.

Debugging a state machine

  • Instrument the trade: Debug.Log the state name on every transition, watch the console flicker at boundaries — a machine that flickers CHASE/PATROL at the range edge is telling you the condition has no hysteresis (a bigger chase-in radius than chase-out radius fixes it; that gap is what 6.3a calls mercy, pointed at AI instead of the player)
  • Reproduce before you theorize: stand where the tester stood, in the state they were in. Most "AI bugs" are boundary bugs at the transition line.
  • Check the guards: a transition that fires every frame is an unguarded if; a transition that never fires is a wrong comparison or a wrong tag. Both are one Debug.Log away.

Where you meet machines this year

  • Patrol / chase / attack / return: 4.5a (drawn), 4.1a–4.4a (built)
  • Cooldowns as clock-machines: 3.3a, 6.3a
  • Climb state (a movement state machine): 7.3a
  • Boss phases: 8.2a (thresholds), 8.4a (attack tables)
  • Turn gates in the card jam: 10.2d
